PRELIMINARY USABILITY FINDING · OWNER-REPORTED

Based on the owner's aggregate study summary, supplied September 21, 2026. Session dates, participant-level timings, completion rates, and task ordering are not available in this case study. These are preliminary findings from a small sample; they do not establish broader outcomes or a causal effect.

The product question

Can an agent help students move from a course shortlist to a usable schedule while keeping their constraints and choices visible? Course planning involves linked lectures and labs, unit targets, overlapping meetings, and personal commitments. The first release focuses on one semester at a time.

The student study tasks described by the owner covered course discovery, perceived relevance to skill goals, course selection, and schedule creation. The app does not independently verify skill development, prerequisites, or degree eligibility.

Decisions you can inspect in the prototype

Review before applying

Multi-course proposals show exact sections and trade-offs. The student chooses which proposal to apply; Undo can reverse the change.

Respect the plan

The scheduler checks linked sections and date-aware time conflicts, protects busy time and locked courses, and rejects stale proposals.

Make the experience easy to try

A labeled guided example generates real schedule options without requiring an agent-compatible browser. It saves into a separate plan.

These describe implemented choices. The available study summary does not identify which changes followed participant feedback.

How it works

The interface and nine native WebMCP tools share one scheduling engine. The synthetic catalog contains 60 courses across two terms. An external browser agent can search courses, inspect sections, read the active plan, and request proposals grounded in that catalog.

The prototype was built with AI assistance using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Plans are stored on the current device. The guided example is deterministic; live agent use requires a compatible browser and agent. There is no university enrollment integration.

Find courses→Check constraints→Review proposals→Student applies

Two kinds of evidence

Usability summary: 20 participants and the mean completion times above were reported by the project owner. The 30% result describes time for the reported workflow. No separate pass rate for conflict-free schedules was supplied.

Functional verification: 23 automated checks passed in the recorded September 16 run. The guided flow, saving a separate plan, and Undo were also exercised in the browser. The WebMCP lab includes 20 of the deterministic checks; three additional demo checks run in the source suite.

Automated checks establish behavior for their test cases. They are not a measure of student satisfaction or agent success across arbitrary requests.

What to measure next

Record individual task times and completion quality, use equivalent tasks with balanced manual/assisted order, and track corrections and unintended changes. That would help distinguish workflow improvement from practice effects and show whether faster completion also preserves schedule quality.
